questions.stem: What is the main purpose of an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)?
options: To record the species living in a national park for a tourism brochure and website
To identify and evaluate a proposal's likely environmental impacts before a decision is made
To repair environmental damage after a development has finished operating and closed
To calculate how much profit a proposed development will make for its owners and its investors
questions.explanation: An EIA predicts and evaluates the likely impacts of a proposed development so decision makers can approve, refuse or set conditions before work begins. It is a planning tool, not a clean-up process after the event.

questions.stem: Why is an EIA carried out before construction rather than after?
options: The law forbids any environmental monitoring once a development has been approved
Impacts can be avoided or reduced by changing the design, site or methods early
Impacts cannot be measured once construction begins, so no data could be collected
Construction always improves the environment, so assessment afterwards is pointless
questions.explanation: Assessing early allows alternatives to be considered, such as moving a road away from a wetland, which is cheaper and more effective than repairing damage later. Monitoring continues during and after construction.

questions.stem: In an EIA, the proponent is:
options: the community group that opposes the development
the consultant who reviews submissions for the court
the person or company proposing the development
the government body that approves or refuses it
questions.explanation: The proponent, or developer, puts forward the proposal and usually prepares the environmental impact statement describing the project, its impacts and how they will be managed. The decision maker is usually a government authority.

questions.stem: Who usually acts as the decision maker in an EIA?
options: An environmental group, after it has made a written submission
A government authority, such as an environment protection agency or minister
The developer, once its own paid consultants have finished writing the whole report
Local residents, by holding a vote at a public meeting near the site
questions.explanation: Government bodies, such as an environment protection authority, a council or a minister, decide whether to approve a proposal and on what conditions. The proponent prepares the assessment but does not approve its own project.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the community in an EIA?
options: To provide local knowledge and raise concerns through submissions and consultation
To prepare the full technical environmental impact statement on behalf of the proponent
To make the final legal decision on whether the development can proceed
To pay for the scientific studies needed to complete the assessment
questions.explanation: Community members and other stakeholders can comment on a draft assessment, contribute local knowledge and raise issues the proponent may have missed. The proponent prepares and funds the studies, and government decides.

questions.stem: In Tasmania, larger polluting proposals classed as Level 2 activities are assessed by the Board of the EPA, and the draft assessment is released for public comment. Why is the public comment period important?
options: It lets the Board avoid collecting any scientific data on the likely impacts
It lets anyone make a written submission that the decision maker must consider
It lets the proponent change the decision after the Board has made it final
It lets the public vote directly to approve or refuse the development proposal
questions.explanation: Public comment allows stakeholders to raise impacts, errors or alternatives, which the Board considers before deciding. It is not a public vote, and it does not replace the scientific assessment of impacts.

questions.stem: Why should consultation with stakeholders begin early in the EIA process?
options: Concerns raised early can shape the design before it is fixed and costly to change
Stakeholders are only allowed to comment before any of the scientific studies are done
Early consultation means the proponent does not need to consult again later
Consultation after approval is illegal, so it must all be done before the project
questions.explanation: Early, genuine consultation lets community knowledge and concerns influence site choice and design, and builds trust. Consultation should continue through the project, not occur once.

questions.stem: A proponent's EIA for a quarry was prepared entirely by consultants it paid, and found only minor impacts. A community group questions the findings. Which step would best address concerns about bias?
options: Independent review of the EIA by the decision maker or outside experts
Asking the same consultants to repeat the study and confirm the results
Approving the quarry immediately so that the dispute does not continue
Removing the community group from the list of stakeholders consulted
questions.explanation: Because the proponent funds the assessment, an independent review by the decision maker or other experts checks that impacts have not been understated. Repeating the work with the same consultants does not remove the potential conflict of interest.

questions.stem: A wind farm is proposed near the coast where a threatened eagle species nests. Which stakeholder pairing correctly matches role to group?
options: Proponent: nearby landholders; decision maker: bird watchers; community: government
Proponent: bird watchers; decision maker: nearby landholders; community: energy company
Proponent: energy company; decision maker: government; community: nearby landholders
Proponent: government; decision maker: energy company; community: bird watchers
questions.explanation: The energy company proposes the project, government assesses and decides, and landholders and interest groups are community stakeholders who are consulted. The eagle would also make the project relevant to threatened species law.

questions.stem: A new road is proposed through a forest that is home to Tasmanian devils and spotted-tailed quolls. Which impact should the EIA give most attention to?
options: Roadkill of wildlife crossing the road, especially at night
Higher rainfall caused by the new road surface across the forest
Increased salinity of the ocean from road construction
Faster growth of rainforest trees beside the road edge
questions.explanation: Roads cause large numbers of wildlife deaths, and devils and quolls feed on carcasses on roads, especially at night. Mitigations such as underpasses, fencing and lower speed limits can be required.

questions.stem: A proposal will clear 20 hectares of native vegetation on a steep slope above a river to build a resort. Which impact is most likely and should be assessed?
options: An increase in the river's dissolved oxygen levels
A reduction in the amount of runoff after storms
Soil erosion and sediment running into the river
A fall in the river's water temperature downstream
questions.explanation: Removing vegetation from steep slopes exposes soil to rain, so erosion and sedimentation of the river are likely. Clearing usually increases, not reduces, runoff after storms.

questions.stem: A proposal is made to expand a marina in an estuary with seagrass beds used as nursery habitat by fish. Which set of impacts should the EIA assess?
options: Increased rainfall, lower air temperatures and reduced sunlight over the catchment
Higher numbers of seagrass shoots, clearer water and more dissolved oxygen nearby
Lower salinity in the open ocean, fewer tides and a decline in upwelling offshore
Dredging plumes smothering seagrass, boat strikes, and fuel and antifouling pollution
questions.explanation: Marina works can stir up sediment that blocks light to seagrass, and boats bring strikes and pollution from fuel and antifouling paints. The other options are not plausible effects of a marina.

questions.stem: A fish farm is proposed in a sheltered bay. Which impact on the environment beneath the pens should the EIA predict and plan to monitor?
options: Build-up of fish waste and uneaten feed on the seabed, lowering oxygen
Increased growth of seagrass directly underneath the shaded floating pens
A rise in the water's salinity caused by fish breathing in the pens
Cooler seabed temperatures caused by the pens reflecting sunlight
questions.explanation: Organic waste and uneaten feed settle under pens, where decomposition uses oxygen and changes benthic communities. Shading reduces, rather than increases, seagrass growth.

questions.stem: Why should an EIA consider cumulative impacts?
options: Several small developments in one area may together cause serious harm
Each development's impact can only be measured once it has finally closed down
Cumulative impacts are always smaller than the impact of one project
Only one development is ever permitted in each river catchment
questions.explanation: A single farm, road or outfall may have a small effect, but many together can exceed what an ecosystem can absorb, such as nutrient loads in an estuary. Assessing each project in isolation can miss this.

questions.stem: What does an Environmental Management Plan (EMP) set out?
options: The list of all species found in Australia and their conservation status
The rules for electing the members of a local council and its committees
The values to be conserved and the strategies to minimise impacts and manage threats
The profits a development will make and how they will be shared among all its owners
questions.explanation: An EMP identifies environmental values to be protected and outlines how impacts and threats will be minimised, monitored and managed. It is a practical working document for a site or project.

questions.stem: In an EMP, an environmental offset is:
options: protecting or restoring habitat elsewhere to compensate for unavoidable loss
a fine paid by a company that breaks the conditions of its approval
a strip of native vegetation left between a development and a nearby waterway
a regular survey that checks whether management is working
questions.explanation: Offsets compensate for residual impacts that cannot be avoided, for example by securing and managing similar habitat on another site. A vegetation strip beside a waterway is a buffer, and a regular survey is monitoring.

questions.stem: Why are offsets usually considered only after other options in an EMP?
options: Impacts should first be avoided, then minimised, with offsets for what remains
Offsets are always much cheaper than changing the design of a development
Offsets fully replace the original habitat immediately and exactly
Offsets remove the need for any monitoring after the project starts
questions.explanation: Good practice is to avoid impacts, then minimise them, and only offset the residual loss, because new or restored habitat may take decades to mature and may never fully match what was lost.

questions.stem: A strip of native vegetation is kept between a new housing estate and a creek. In an EMP this is an example of:
options: stakeholder consultation
environmental buffering
an environmental offset
a legislative requirement
questions.explanation: A buffer separates a sensitive area from a source of impact, here filtering runoff and reducing disturbance to the creek. An offset compensates for loss at another site.

questions.stem: Why must an EMP include ongoing monitoring?
options: To check whether strategies are working so management can be adjusted
To prove the original EIA was correct so that no changes are ever needed
To replace the need for any baseline data before the project began
To count only the number of visitors so that fees can be collected
questions.explanation: Monitoring compares conditions against baseline data and targets, showing whether management is effective. If impacts are worse than predicted, management can be changed, which is called adaptive management.

questions.stem: Why does an EMP list the legislative requirements that apply to a site?
options: So managers know which laws and permit conditions they must comply with
So the site can ignore laws that are not written into the plan
So the government no longer needs to enforce environmental laws
So the plan can replace the need for an environmental impact assessment
questions.explanation: Listing obligations under laws such as the EPBC Act or Tasmania's Threatened Species Protection Act 1995 ensures that managers meet permit conditions and protect listed species. The plan does not override the law.

questions.stem: A national park EMP includes regular meetings with local residents, bushwalking clubs and tourism operators. Which EMP element is this?
options: Environmental buffering
Legislative requirements
Stakeholder consultation
Environmental offsetting
questions.explanation: Meeting with groups who use or are affected by the park is stakeholder consultation, which helps managers understand concerns and gain support for management. Offsets and buffers are physical strategies on the ground.

questions.stem: A coastal reserve's EMP identifies nesting shorebirds as a key value. Which strategy best protects them?
options: Seasonal fencing and signs that keep people and dogs away from nesting areas
Building a large car park on the dunes so that visitors can see the nests up close
Removing all native dune vegetation to give the birds more open space
Allowing off-leash dogs on the beach during the breeding season
questions.explanation: Beach-nesting birds are disturbed by people and dogs, which can cause nests to fail. Temporary fencing, signs and dog restrictions during the breeding season reduce this threat.

questions.stem: Reserve A is a small urban bushland patch with heavy visitor use. Reserve B is a large remote wilderness area. Which comparison of EMP strategies is most appropriate?
options: A and B need exactly the same strategies because all reserves face exactly the same threats
A focuses on track hardening and weed control; B focuses on fire management and minimal-impact access
A focuses on large prescribed burns across the whole patch; B focuses on building sealed car parks
A focuses on closing it to all visitors forever; B focuses on encouraging off-road vehicle use
questions.explanation: Small urban reserves face trampling, edge effects and weeds, so hardened tracks and weed control suit them. Large remote areas face threats such as wildfire and the impacts of walkers, so fire management and minimal-impact access suit them better.

questions.stem: A walking track in an alpine national park has widened into a muddy, eroded strip as walkers step around wet sections. Which EMP strategy is most specific and relevant?
options: Increase visitor numbers so the track becomes compacted and dries out faster
Remove all of the track signs so that fewer walkers can find the track and use it
Plant fast-growing introduced grasses along the edges to hold the soil
Build a raised boardwalk over the wet sections and revegetate the widened edges
questions.explanation: Boardwalks keep walkers on a defined path over boggy ground, stopping further widening, and revegetating with local native species repairs the damage. Introduced grasses could become weeds in an alpine area.

questions.stem: Which feature makes a suggestion for an EMP specific and relevant rather than vague?
options: It names a threat, an action and how its success will be measured
It states that the environment should be looked after carefully
It recommends that more research be done at some point in the future
It says that everyone should try harder to protect the site
questions.explanation: A useful EMP strategy is practical and measurable, for example 'fence the creek to exclude stock and monitor bank vegetation cover each year'. General statements give managers nothing to act on.

questions.stem: Phytophthora cinnamomi, a soil pathogen that kills many native plants, has been found near a walking track in a reserve. Which EMP strategy best reduces its spread?
options: Encourage walkers to explore off-track so that they spread out over a much wider area
Water the affected area heavily so that the plants can recover more quickly
Move soil from the infected area to other parts of the reserve to dilute it
Install boot-cleaning stations and keep vehicles and walkers to clean, dry tracks
questions.explanation: The pathogen is spread in soil and water, including on boots and vehicles, so hygiene stations and keeping to defined tracks limit its movement. Moving soil or creating wet conditions would help it spread.

questions.stem: A mine EMP requires topsoil to be stockpiled during construction and spread back over the site at closure, followed by planting local native species. Which aim does this mainly serve?
options: Buffering the creek from runoff while the mine is still being operated
Rehabilitating the site so native vegetation can re-establish after mining
Increasing the mine's output by storing the topsoil for later sale as construction fill
Offsetting the clearing by protecting a separate site in another region
questions.explanation: Topsoil holds seeds, nutrients and soil organisms, so returning it and planting local species helps the site recover after mining. An offset protects habitat on a different site, which is not what this strategy does.

questions.stem: Why should EMP monitoring results be compared with baseline data?
options: Baseline data are collected after closure, so they show the project's final outcome
Baseline data replace the need to collect any further monitoring data
Baseline data are used only to work out the cost of the development
Baseline data show conditions before the project, so change can be measured
questions.explanation: Comparing monitoring with pre-development conditions shows whether impacts are occurring and how large they are. Without a baseline, changes cannot be attributed to the project.

questions.stem: Monitoring under a fish farm EMP shows dissolved oxygen near the seabed has fallen below the trigger level in the plan. What should happen next under good management?
options: Management responds, for example by reducing stocking or fallowing the lease
Monitoring stops, because the trigger level set in the plan has already been reached
The trigger level is lowered so that the farm appears to comply again
Nothing changes, because the farm already holds a government licence
questions.explanation: Trigger levels are set so that management acts when impacts exceed acceptable limits, such as cutting fish numbers or resting the site to let the seabed recover. Changing the trigger to hide a problem defeats the purpose of monitoring.

questions.stem: A proposed dam would flood the habitat of a threatened freshwater crayfish. The EIA finds that the impact cannot be avoided. Which EMP measure is most appropriate?
options: Ignore the crayfish because the dam will supply water to a growing population
Build a strip of native vegetation around the new dam wall to act as an environmental buffer
Release the crayfish into a city stormwater drain where they will be out of the way
Offset by protecting and restoring crayfish habitat in a nearby catchment, with monitoring
questions.explanation: When loss is unavoidable, an offset secures and improves equivalent habitat elsewhere, and monitoring checks that the population there is thriving. A buffer at the dam wall would not replace flooded habitat.

questions.stem: Which item best belongs in the 'resources to be managed' section of a forest reserve EMP?
options: The number of staff cars parked at the reserve visitor centre each day
The price of tickets charged at the reserve's gift shop
The colour scheme used on the reserve's printed brochures
Old-growth trees with hollows used by nesting birds and possums
questions.explanation: An EMP identifies environmental values and resources to be conserved, such as hollow-bearing trees, which take many decades to form and are vital habitat. Parking, prices and brochures are not environmental resources.

questions.stem: How do an EIA and an EMP differ?
options: An EIA predicts impacts before approval; an EMP sets out how they will be managed
An EIA is written after site closure; an EMP is written before the proposal is lodged
An EIA protects threatened species; an EMP protects only the developer's profits
An EIA is a community vote; an EMP is a court ruling on a development dispute
questions.explanation: The EIA assesses likely impacts to inform the approval decision, while the EMP is the working plan for managing impacts and values during construction, operation and closure. The two often go together.

questions.stem: A council's EMP for a river reserve reports that weed cover fell from 40% to 15% over five years, but platypus sightings did not change. What is the best evaluation?
options: Weed cover data are unreliable because they changed while platypus data stayed the same
Weed control is working, but the platypus target may need a different strategy or better monitoring
The whole EMP has failed, because platypus sightings did not rise at all over the five years
The EMP has fully succeeded, so monitoring of both weeds and platypus can now stop
questions.explanation: The weed target shows clear progress, while unchanged platypus sightings suggest that strategy needs review, or that casual sightings are a poor measure. Evaluating each strategy against its own target allows adaptive management.

questions.stem: Why should an EMP be reviewed and updated regularly?
options: New threats, monitoring results and changes in law may require new strategies
Laws require every EMP to be completely rewritten each month by the developer
Once written, an EMP can never be changed, so reviews only confirm it
Reviews allow the plan to drop all monitoring once construction has ended
questions.explanation: Conditions change: new pests or diseases arrive, monitoring reveals unexpected impacts and laws are amended. Regular review keeps strategies effective, which is the basis of adaptive management.

questions.stem: A solar farm is proposed on cleared farmland next to a large patch of native grassland that contains a threatened plant. Which EMP strategy most directly protects the grassland during construction?
options: Mow the whole grassland short so that machinery can cross it more easily
Plant introduced pasture grasses around the panels to suppress native weeds
Fence off the grassland and keep machinery, stockpiles and access tracks outside it
Spread the construction stockpiles across the grassland to reduce their height
questions.explanation: Physical exclusion stops machinery, soil and materials damaging the threatened plant and its habitat. Mowing, stockpiling or planting introduced grasses would degrade the grassland it is meant to protect.

questions.stem: A hydro-electric dam is proposed on a river with platypus and native fish downstream. Which downstream impact should the EIA assess?
options: A rise in ocean salinity at the river mouth caused by the turbines spinning
Higher rainfall downstream caused by evaporation from the new storage lake
Faster growth of rainforest on ridges far above the river in the catchment
Changed timing and volume of river flows, altering habitat and fish migration
questions.explanation: Dams store and release water on a different schedule from natural flows and block fish passage, changing downstream habitat. Environmental flow releases and fishways are common conditions.
